summary: This informational memo describes research challenges for Information-Centric Networking (ICN), an approach where uniquely named data, rather than host locations, is the core Internet principle. Data becomes independent of where it is stored or how it travels. The document surveys open problems that researchers would need to address.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you ask a specific shop for a book. In this idea, you just ask for the book by its name and anyone nearby who has a copy can hand it over. This lists the hard problems still to solve.

questions: what is a named data object
route by name vs lookup by name
subtitle: A research-group survey of the open technical problems in building networks around named data instead of host addresses.

tldr.problem: Today's Internet moves packets between hosts, so content distribution networks and peer-to-peer systems have to do data-centric work in overlays that the network cannot see. This leaves paths sub-optimal and multicast underused, and makes authenticity hard to check.
tldr.mechanism: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) makes uniquely named data objects a first-class network service, so any node can forward requests, cache objects and validate them by name. The RFC catalogs the research challenges this raises, from naming and security to routing, mobility, caching and management.
tldr.outcome: It is a research agenda and does not define a standard. It records technical challenges and current approaches for future work, and leaves business challenges to another document.

today: RFC 7927 is an Informational research-group document from July 2016, with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed for it. It states that it does not constitute a standard.

sections.title: Problems with Host-Centric Communication
sections.content:
Content distribution networks (CDNs) and peer-to-peer (P2P) applications already give a service of accessing named data objects, but they live in overlays, so the network does not know about data requests. The RFC lists the consequences: traffic follows paths set by the overlay topology, multicast and broadcast go underused so the same object is requested and delivered many times, overlays need heavy infrastructure that can prevent local direct communication, and the forwarding layer cannot cooperate with transport functions such as local retransmission.

Provenance checks also rely on host authentication, so a locally cached copy is hard to validate. Many applications also reinvent caching, replication and authenticity checks even though they share a similar model for accessing named data.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, each app builds its own delivery trick on top of a network that does not understand what is being delivered. That wastes effort and trips over itself.

sections.title: ICN Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
A Named Data Object (NDO) is an addressable unit of data with a name bound to it, usually with a way to secure that binding. A Requestor asks the network for an NDO, and a Publisher makes an NDO available so requests can reach it; the publisher need not be the creator.

ICN names represent data, not nodes or interfaces, and they drive forwarding and matching of requests to responses. Name-content binding validation is a fundamental security service available to any node, not only the requestor. Since bindings can be checked, every ICN node can cache objects and answer requests without proving its own identity, which allows sharing, robustness and local retransmissions.

Retrieval is typically controlled by the requestor, so ICN transport tends to be receiver-driven: the requestor sets the rate by regulating requests, and retransmits by resending them. Sessions need not be end to end, because caches may answer.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything has a name, and anyone can check that a copy matches its name. So any helper on the way can keep copies and pass them along safely.

sections.title: Naming and Security Challenges
sections.content:
Names must be unique and long-lived, and because objects can be cached anywhere the origin can no longer be trusted. Two naming families are described: hierarchical names, similar to URIs, that help routing aggregation and may be human readable, and hash-based names that bind the hash of the content (or the publisher's public key, with a signature) to the name, so integrity can be checked without a PKI. The latter are typically flat and not human readable. RFC 6920 specifies a naming format using content hashes.

Naming challenges include dynamic objects named before they exist (such as live streams), requestor privacy because the network can see and log requests, updating and versioning when a name-content binding must not change, and managing accessibility.

On security, the RFC notes TLS (RFC 5246) cannot be the general solution since the channel endpoint is not trusted. Open problems include distributing publisher public keys (via hierarchical PKI or hash-based names), binding objects to real-world identities, access control (a separated approach using a third party versus an integrated approach using encryption and key distribution), encryption, aggregated requests versus per-requestor filtering, state overloading attacks such as interest flooding, loss of control when serving from replicas, cryptographic robustness for publishers who sign massive amounts of long-lived content, and growth of routing and forwarding tables as an attack vector.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can hand you a copy, you need a way to check it is the real one. The hard parts are keeping the checks cheap, keeping things private, and stopping people from overloading the helpers.

sections.title: Routing, Mobility and Wireless
sections.content:
ICN routing may have three steps: name resolution, discovery and delivery. Combining them gives three styles. Route-By-Name Routing (RBNR) skips resolution and routes on the name directly, which cuts latency but can make routing tables proportional to the number of objects unless names aggregate. Lookup-By-Name Routing (LBNR) first resolves a name to a locator, so it needs a resolution system with fast lookup and fast update. Hybrid Routing (HR) mixes them, for example RBNR inside a domain and LBNR between domains.

On mobility, IP uses mobility anchors and tunnels. The RFC says this is not the best way forward for ICN, and that no solution yet gives a definite answer on mobility with native ICN primitives. Mobile content sources are harder than mobile clients.

On wireless, the RFC uses a meeting example in which notes cross the wireless medium at least N+1 times for N participants, because broadcast is turned into virtual unicast channels. Caching at the access point would not remove that waste. It asks how ICN can exploit the broadcast nature of wireless.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a thing by name is like finding a book without knowing which shelf it is on. Moving around and sharing Wi-Fi make it harder, but also offer chances to do better.

sections.title: Congestion Control, Caching and Management
sections.content:
For rate and congestion control, a requestor can fetch from several sources and regulate its request rate. But sub-flows from caches make measurements such as round-trip time misleading and can cause false timeouts, out-of-order delivery is expected, and request aggregation makes fairness and retransmission handling hard because a router cannot tell how many requestors sit behind one request.

In-network caching raises questions of cache placement (on-path versus off-path, with on-path needing line-speed operation), content placement and redundant copies, routing requests to caches, detecting stale objects (directly through information such as a timestamp in the name, or indirectly by asking the publisher), and sharing caches across applications without cache poisoning.

Network management tools today are node-centric or end-to-end, so ICN needs its own, and the RFC suggests using native ICN mechanisms such as in-network storage and publish/subscribe for monitoring and notifications. Application sections also cover web applications, video and the Internet of Things, where ICN's receiver-driven model makes push-style publishing hard.
sections.plainLanguage: When copies live in many places, it is harder to know how fast things are going, which copy is fresh, and how to look after the whole system.
